title: Dawn-dusk Asymmetrical Distribution of Saturn’s Cusp

paper_content.abstract: Saturn’s magnetosphere, shaped by solar wind interaction with its dipole field, differs from Earth’s due to faster rotation and Enceladus’s internal plasma sources. An ongoing focus of investigation is how the internal plasma sources and rapid rotation result in a different global magnetospheric configuration. The magnetospheric cusp, a crucial interaction region between solar wind and planetary magnetic field, serves as an indicator of global magnetic configuration. Here we utilize Cassini observations from 2004 to 2010 to study dawn-dusk asymmetry in Saturn’s cusp distribution and extend the number of cusp events from about 11 reported in previous studies to 67. We find peak occurrence in the post-noon sector and signatures extending to post-dusk (near 20 local time), resembling recent observations of Jupiter’s post-dusk cusp. We further examine magnetic topology using high-resolution magnetohydrodynamics simulations to visualize the cusp asymmetry. This is consistent with previous studies, but our simulations provide a more detailed view of Saturn’s magnetic topology near the magnetopause. This asymmetry of cusp distribution demonstrates how rapid rotation and internal plasma sources fundamentally alter magnetospheric configuration, offering insights for understanding other rotating planetary systems within and beyond the solar system.
paper_content.introduction:
Planetary magnetospheres are formed as a result of the continuous interaction between the high-speed solar wind and the internally generated magnetic fields present in most planets within the solar system, which display considerable variations among different planets. For example, the magnetospheres of Jupiter and Saturn are more internally driven because of the planets’ rapid rotation speeds coupled with internal plasma sources within their magnetospheres, which differs from the strongly solar wind-driven magnetospheres typically seen on Earth1,2. In the case of ice giants like Uranus and Neptune, the unique pole-on configuration of their magnetospheres – the geometry in which the upstream solar-wind flow is approximately aligned with the planet’s magnetic dipole axis – lead to distinct coupling dynamics with the solar wind3,4. Atthesametime,the highly dynamic nature of these gas giants’ plasma environments fosters complex interactions with the solar wind, which serves as an external factor in the magnetospheric dynamics5,6. Understanding these diverse magnetospheric dynamics can improve the interpretation of observations of planetary systems and offer useful perspectives for the broader field of planetary science, including star-planet interactions.

When the solar wind interacts with a planetary magnetosphere, magnetic reconnection on the magnetopause often occurs where the magnetic shear is sufficiently large. At Earth, magnetopause reconnection is strongly governed by the north–south component of the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF)—with southward IMF driving subsolar reconnection and northward IMF favoring high-latitude lobe reconnection7. In the rotationally dominated magnetospheres of giant planets, magnetopause reconnection was reported to be favored at high latitudes. In contrast, low-latitude subsolar reconnection is often suppressed by diamagnetic effects and is therefore less likely to occur there8–10. Recent simulations11–13 have suggested that reconnection at Jupiter is strongly influenced by the east–west IMF component, with reconnection occurring predominantly at high latitudes and suppressed reconnection at low-latitude magnetopause locations. During reconnection, solar wind particles are allowed to enter the magnetosphere through the newly reconnected magnetic field lines. The magnetospheric cusp is known as a vital funnel-shaped region that permit these particles to directly access the atmosphere14,15. The cusps play a crucial role in planetary magnetospheres, as they significantly contribute to various mass and energy transport processes within the magnetosphere, ionosphere, and upper atmosphere. These processes are key in the formation of geomagnetic storms16, substorms17, and auroras18. A series of in situ studies, e.g., using the Cluster multi-spacecraft mission, have revealed that Earth’s cusp is a broad, complex region characterized by various intriguing boundary layers14,19. The cusp in Earth’s quiescent magnetosphere, strongly governed by solar wind, typically exhibits a general morning-afternoon symmetry of its morphology and statistical occurrence rates, which is one of the most fundamental properties of terrestrial cusp20,21, although the distribution of its spatial location can be influenced by the IMF By component and pressure of the solar wind22,23. In contrast, due to Saturn’s rapid rotation, the Kronian magnetospheric plasma generally subcorotates relative to the planet, remaining in near-rigid corotation within approximately 20 Rs, but falling significantly below the rigid corotation rate beyond Titan’s orbit24,25. Compared to Earth, Jupiter exhibits bright and persistent polar auroras26, and Saturn’s aurora shows variable morphologies resembling both Earth-like and Jupiter-like structures27, suggesting a markedly different magnetospheric configuration and dynamics of rapidly rotating giant planets2,28,29. The rapid rotation of giant planets plays a crucial role in modifying magnetic flux transport within the magnetosphere and near the magnetopause compared to Earth12,29. This rotational influence can modify dawnside magnetopause reconnection rates associated with solar wind interaction and alter the configuration of the magnetopause and the open–closed field line boundary, where the cusps are anchored12,29.

Zhang et al.11,29 provide additional insights into the distinct magnetospheric configurations of Earth and giant planets using high-resolution simulations. In rotation-dominated Jovian-like systems, low reconnection rates on the dawn side can cause closed flux to accumulate there, resulting in an open flux fraction of approximately 20% in the polar region (above 80° magnetic latitude, MLAT20). Conversely, a terrestrial-like magnetosphere is mostly solar wind-dominated, exhibiting near-complete openness of the polar region above 80° MLAT (about 98%)29. Although Saturn’s magnetosphere is similarly rotation-dominated, its weak magnetic field (an equatorial magnetic field strength of 0.21 G, about 1/20 of Jupiter’s30) results in its reduced corotation dominance. The consequently higher solar wind merging potential-to-corotation potential ratio (0.38 at Saturn vs. 0.09 at Jupiter29) increases solar wind-driven flux opening efficiency. As a result, Kronian-like magnetosphere’s polar open flux fraction varies widely (58–93% above 80° MLAT)29. Observationally, Saturn’s high-latitude magnetosphere has been reported to be largely plasma-depleted and composed predominantly of open field lines, with the polar cap boundary located at 14.5 ± 0.6° and 12.7 ± 0.6° colatitude in the southern and northern hemispheres, respectively31,32. Compared to Jupiter’s small open flux area, Saturn’s relatively large area of open magnetic field may result in a more observable cusp, although more detailed analysis and observations are needed to confirm the prediction. Previous theoretical models by Cowley et al. (2004, 2005)33,34 proposed that rotational dynamics drive the subsolar X-line at Saturn, thereby influencing the azimuthal distribution of the polar cap and cusp in local time. This framework is based on terrestrial magnetopause reconnection pictures and the Dungey7/Vasyliūnas cycle35. However, the applicability of the Dungey cycle to giant planets remains a topic of active debate36.

Currently, the global distribution picture of Saturn’s cusp remains an active topic of ongoing research. As shown in the simple schematic Fig. 1, a comparative analysis of Saturn’s cusp distribution with Earth’s is crucial for understanding the diverse planetary magnetospheres and their interaction with the solar wind.

Some case studies have identified characteristics in Saturn’s cusp region, such as magnetosheath-like electron features and ion dispersion patterns that are similar to those observed in Earth’s cusp37–40. Additionally, variations in ion dispersion features under different reconnection conditions and magnetic depression features in Saturn’s cusp have been examined, revealing parallels with Earth’s cusp37,38,40. These similarities indicate that the microphysical processes governing the behavior of charged particles within cusps might be universal across different planetary environments. However, the study by Arridge et al.40 noted cusp encounters recurring in sync with Saturn’s rotation period, thought to be linked to the cusp position oscillating in phase with Saturn’s global magnetospheric dynamics40. Previous research utilizing global magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations has demonstrated that the magnetospheric structure of rapidly rotating giant planets exhibits significant asymmetries41, markedly different from those observed at Earth11,12. For instance, simulation studies have shown that rapid rotation significantly alters the global magnetospheric configuration of Jupiter, notably causing a pronounced duskward shift in the open magnetic field regions associated with Jupiter’s polar cusp11,12. This dusk-side distribution of Jupiter’s cusp has been supported by observational results from Xu et al. (2024)13. Given Saturn’s rotation-dominated magnetosphere, a similar duskward shift in its cusp distribution is expected13,29.

However, several questions remain unresolved. A comprehensive global observational picture of cusp regions at giant planets is still lacking. At Jupiter, due to Juno’s current orbital constraints13,42,43, high-latitude observations in the middle-to-outer magnetosphere across various local times remain incomplete, leaving the properties and distribution of cusp regions in the dawn, noon, and post-noon sectors mysterious. Given Saturn’s similarly rapidly rotating magnetosphere, investigating its global cusp distribution is especially important. Such research provides valuable comparative insight into Jupiter’s reported dusk-side cusp and informs future observations of Jupiter’s cusp and high-latitude boundary layer regions. Previous studies have provided valuable analyses of several Saturn cusp events37–40. Here we extend this foundation by offering a global, dwell-time–normalized statistical view, enabling a global assessment of the cusp occurrence distribution.

In the present research, we explored the global distribution of Saturn’s cusp using data from the Cassini spacecraft, spanning from 2004 to 2010. Additionally, we employed high-resolution MHD simulations11,12,44 to visualize the magnetic configurations of Saturn and its cusp, revealing Saturn’s magnetopause-related three-dimensional magnetic topology. Both the statistical analysis and the simulation results highlight the characteristics of the morning-afternoon asymmetry in Saturn’s cusp, which diverges from the symmetric distribution observed at Earth and shows consistency with Jupiter’s recently discovered configuration.
paper_content.results:
A Kronian cusp case is presented for the period between 23:00 on January 30 and 05:00 on January 31, 2009, when the Cassini spacecraft was located in the high latitude (>40°) noon region of the northern hemisphere, near 16 Rs (Fig. 2). Cassini transitioned from the magnetospheric region to the boundary layer and the cusp region, as shown in Fig. 2. In this study, we examine Cassini’s in-situ measurements from three key sources: the Cassini Magnetometer instrument (MAG)45, Cassini Plasma Spectrometer - Electron Spectrometer (CAPS-ELS)46, and Cassini Plasma Spectrometer - Ion Mass Spectrometer (CAPS-IMS)46. Before 23:51 UT, as indicated by the first dashed line in Fig. 2, Cassini recorded a magnetospheric electron spectrum with enhanced energy ranges between 1000 and 10000 eV. In this region, the ion energy spectrum displayed no distinct features, and the electron pitch angle distribution was isotropic. These characteristics are indicative of the magnetosphere at this location30,40; hence, this region is identified as part of the magnetosphere and is denoted by the letter M in Fig. 2.

After 00:36 UT marked by the second dashed line in Fig. 2, the spacecraft observed a region characterized by a notable enhancement in the electron energy spectrum from 10 to 100 eV, as depicted in Fig. 2c. This enhancement is characteristic of magnetosheath electrons47. Concurrently, the magnetic field component remained relatively stable, as shown in Fig. 2a, b, which rules out the possibility of the spacecraft being in the magnetosheath. Additionally, observations included a bidirectional distribution of low-energy electrons and a rise in high-energy electrons opposing the magnetic field direction (shown in Fig. 2e–h), along with multiple ion dispersion signals. These observations suggest that the magnetopause experienced pulsed reconnection processes37,48. These distinct features robustly indicate that the region encountered by the spacecraft is indeed a magnetospheric cusp region37,38,40. Situated between the magnetosphere and the cusp is a transitional area, characterized by plasma properties that are intermediate between those of the magnetosphere and the cusp. This region is identified as a boundary layer and is denoted by BL in Fig. 2.

To identify Kronian cusp events, the most important criteria, based on previous research on Saturn’s cusp37,38,40 and Jupiter’s cusp13, are as follows: (1) Spacecraft location, e.g., relatively high latitudes (>30 degrees) and within the magnetopause; (2) Most typical plasma characteristics within cusp regions, e.g., magnetosheath-like electron energy distributions13,37,38,40. These are the Level 1 criteria, the most critical for identification. Most Saturn cusp events can be well identified by meeting these criteria. Additionally, other important but non-essential features can further aid in identification, including ion dispersion37,40 associated with magnetopause reconnection, field-aligned electron distributions37,40, and magnetic depressions39 within cusp regions. These are referred to as the Level 2 criteria, which can be helpful but are not necessary for cusp identification. Utilizing all these criteria, we identified a total of 67 cusp events that matched the characteristics observed by the Cassini spacecraft between 2004 and 2010. These events encompass previously reported cases of Saturn’s cusp region, demonstrating the reliability of our identification and the consistency of this study with prior research. Information on Saturn’s cusp events and the corresponding criteria fulfillment is organized in the Supplementary Data 1. It is noted that the survey period of 2004–2010 corresponds to the timeframe from Cassini’s entry into Saturn’s bow shock to the final year before the CAPS instrument was placed in Operations on Hold (2011)38. Since the detection of magnetosheath-like electron spectra by CAPS provides the most direct and essential evidence for cusp identification14,20,40, data collected after 2011 were excluded to ensure the reliability of event identification. This study does not distinguish between cusp types associated with different magnetopause reconnection pictures. Recent findings suggest that magnetopause reconnection at giant planets may be significantly more complex than the subsolar/lobe-dominated patterns observed at Earth, with reconnection-related dynamics exhibiting greater variability11–13. Moreover, long-term, stable solar wind measurements are lacking at Saturn during the Cassini mission39,40, and solar wind models cannot provide real-time, accurate information on the east–west and north–south components of IMF39,40,49. As a result, identifying cusp types based on ion dispersion signatures linked to specific reconnection geometries is highly challenging and beyond the scope of this study.

The global distribution of these events is presented in Fig. 3. Fig. 3a and b demonstrate that the majority of observed cusp events are located in the northern hemisphere and predominantly on the afternoon side, with some events even detectable on the post-dusk side (after 20 local time, LT). Fig. 3c displays the distribution of cusp events at high latitudes (>30° or <-30°) across various radial distances and local times. Due to the Cassini spacecraft’s trajectory constraints, its high-latitude path in the southern hemisphere is primarily on the morning side, while in the northern hemisphere, it is largely on the afternoon side. Notably, between radial distances of 10 and 20 Rs, high-latitude tracks are present on both the morning and afternoon sides. However, there is a marked contrast in event density for 10 to 20 Rs radial range in high latitudes (Fig. 3c). Between 13 and 16 LT, a total of 17 cusp events were identified within Cassini’s accumulated dwell time of 36,626 minutes, corresponding to an event density of approximately 0.028 events per hour. In contrast, during the interval from 8 to 11 LT with a dwell time of 37,379 minutes, only 4 cusp events were detected, indicating a substantially lower event density of 0.006 events/hour. Although previous studies have reported minor differences in the period of kilometric radiation waves north and south of Saturn50,51, there is currently insufficient evidence to suggest a pronounced north-south asymmetry in Saturn’s magnetospheric configuration that can notably impact the polar cusp structure. Thus, this study posits that the observed distribution reflects the morning and afternoon asymmetry in Saturn’s cusp distribution. More importantly, three post-dusk cusp events were identified during the statistical study, with the specific identification criteria for each event detailed in Supplementary Data 1. And comprehensive plasma analyses, along with comparisons distinguishing these events from nightside ionospheric outflows, are provided in Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Figs. 1–3. The plasma energy spectra and spatial distributions of these events closely resemble those observed in Jupiter’s post-dusk polar cusp region as reported by Xu et al. (2024) (see Supplementary Note 1), indicating a consistent cusp microphysics and complex magnetospheric structures across different giant planets.

To quantify this asymmetry, we computed the probability distribution of the cusp with the time resolution of 1 minute, as depicted in Fig. 4b. Additionally, for comparative purposes with Saturn, we replicated Earth’s cusp probability distribution using the Cluster electron and magnetic field datasets52 as shown in Fig. 4a. It is noted that the cusp detections at different local times are normalized by the spacecraft’s high-latitude dwell time at corresponding local times for both Cluster and Cassini, minimizing potential statistical biases caused by orbital differences. For detailed information on event identification and case presentations in Earth’s cusp region, please refer to Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Fig. 4. The results of this distribution are consistent with previous studies20: The peak occurrence rate of Earth’s cusp is centered around noon (11-13 LT), with some disparity between the morning and afternoon sides, which can be attributed to the influence of the IMF By component and solar wind dynamic pressure, which can shift and modify the cusp’s position during spacecraft observation22,23. In contrast, the peak occurrence rate of Saturn’s cusp manifests on the afternoon side 13-15 LT. Notably, Saturn’s cusp distribution does not mirror the shift of Earth’s cusp distribution toward the afternoon under positive IMF By condition22. Instead, it shows a clear shift in overall distribution toward the dusk or even the night side. Global MHD simulations11,29,44, as illustrated in Fig. 4c and 4d, map the magnetic field configurations near the magnetopauses of Earth and Saturn, highlighting the differences between their distributions. Saturn’s magnetopause, influenced by the planet’s rapid rotational dynamics, is more expanded on the morning side compared to the afternoon side, in agreement with previous MHD simulations and observations, which found the magnetopause was typically expanded by 1-2 Rs on the dawn side compared to dusk41,53,54. The cusp must conform to this topology, leading to the observed asymmetry and enabling cusp observation even on the post-dusk side — an occurrence hardly seen at Earth20,22. Moreover, the simulation results reveal a picture of Saturn’s magnetopause reconnection under typical solar wind conditions, which closely resembles that of Jupiter12,13. Reconnection occurs predominantly at high latitudes and is suppressed in low-latitude magnetopause regions—unlike Earth, where reconnection is primarily governed by the north–south component of the interplanetary magnetic field7,14,55. For a detailed presentation and analysis of Saturn’s magnetopause reconnection results, please refer to Supplementary Note 3 and Supplementary Figs. 5–6.
paper_content.methods:
Simulation information
In this study, the global MHD model of Saturn’s magnetic configuration (Fig. 4d) is built upon the GAMERA code (Grid Agnostic MHD for Extended Research Applications) to tackle equations on a specifically designed curvilinear, non-orthogonal grid suited for the study of planetary magnetospheres44. The computational model employs a 256 × 256 × 256-cell grid, implemented as a non uniform, distorted spherical grid oriented along the Solar Magnetic (SM) X-axis and possessing a symmetry axis. The grid exhibits non-uniformity in the radial-azimuthal plane, with cell sizes reducing as they approach Saturn. The simulation begins at an inner boundary of 4 Rs, with boundary conditions obtained from electrostatic potential models61,62. The outer boundary takes the form of a cylinder, stretching from SM-X = 56 Rs to SM-X = -600 Rs, with a radius around 214 Rs. The conditions at this outer boundary are controlled by the solar wind and the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF). The grid is structured so that its resolution diminishes with increasing distance from Saturn, which enhances computational efficiency by aligning with the larger scale of magnetospheric processes farther from the planet. The radial cell sizes near Saturn’s magnetopause range between approximately 0.1 and 0.2 Rs. This model is driven by simplified representations of solar wind and IMF conditions, setting IMF Bz at -0.5 nT, a particle density of 0.1 per cubic centimeter, a solar wind velocity of 400 km/s. The dipole tilt of Saturn’s magnetic field is maintained at 0 degrees to remove hemispheric asymmetries, thereby simplifying the overall analysis. Moreover, the moon Enceladus ejects plasma into Saturn’s magnetosphere63,64, creating an internal plasma source that migrates outward and influences the magnetopause. The simulation data presented in this paper are publicly available online via Xu (2026)65.

Cassini and cluster data
We analyzed magnetometer (MAG), electron spectrometer (ELS), and ion mass spectrometer (IMS) data from the Cassini spacecraft spanning 2004-2010. Data were obtained from the NASA Planetary Data System. We analyzed magnetic field observations and position data from the Cassini MAG instrument45, and thermal ion and electron measurements with energy ranges up to 28 keV (electrons) and 50 keV (ions) from Cassini-CAPS/IMS/ELS46. Cluster magnetic field and particle data were obtained from the ESA Cluster Science Archive. The datasets to analyze Earth’s cusp were obtained by the FGM66, PEACE67, CIS68, and WHISPER69 instruments onboard Cluster. Detailed identification information of Earth’s cusp is shown in Supplementary Note 2.

Data availability
All Cassini data presented here are publicly available from NASA’s Planetary Data System (https://pds-ppi.igpp.ucla.edu/). The MAG dataset of Cassini is available via https://search-pdsppi.igpp.ucla.edu/search/view/?f=yes&id=pds://PPI/cassini-mag-cal. The CAPS dataset of Cassini is available via https://search-pdsppi.igpp.ucla.edu/search/?sc=Cassini&i=CAPS. The Cluster data used in this paper can be obtained from the Cluster Science Archive via https://csa.esac.esa.int/csa-web/. The simulation data of Saturn’s magnetospheric topology presented in this paper are publicly available online via Xu (2026)65 https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/RQJYH. The datasets generated during and/or analysed during the current study are available from the corresponding author upon request.

Code availability
The Cassini data are processed and analyzed using the Spedas package70, which can be downloaded via the https://github.com/spedaspage. The presentation of simulated data can be done using standard plotting libraries (Python/Matlab), for example, the Python library matplotlib (which can be downloaded via the https://matplotlib.org/stable/install/page). The Matlab code used in the analysis of simulations is publicly available online via Xu (2026)65 https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/RQJYH.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The paper written by Xu, Yao et al., summarizes a new list of cusp crossings identified at Saturn’s magnetosphere, providing an updated list of this high latitude phenomenon. The papers results discuss possible dawn-dusk asymmetries in the magnetosphere, that add to the substantial body of evidence from a large number of previous papers, that Saturn is a rotationally driven magnetosphere and produces dawn-dusk asymmetries.

Originality and significance: although this paper provides a contribution to the field of Saturn’s magnetosphere, it is not however a contribution commensurate to the standards of Nature Communications which requires the results to be of high significance and “important to the field and advance understanding in a way that will move the field forward” - but instead this work is incremental. The results do not move the field forward but instead build on established work that has previously shown that a) that cusp plasma occurs after dayside magnetopause reconnection at Saturn (e.g. Jasinski et al., 2014, 2016), b) that there is dawn-dusk asymmetries in the cusp (e.g. Arridge et al., 2016) and c) that Saturn is rotationally driven and displays dawn-dusk asymmetries generally (e.g. Pilkington et al., 2015; Jia & Kivelson, 2016; Wilson et al., 2013; Sergis et al., 2015; Allen et al., 2018).

It is suggested that a more appropriate journal for this publication, would be AGU’s Journal of Geophysical Research.

There are other issues regarding originality. Below are a list of strengths and weaknesses of the paper; with the weaknesses outweighing the strengths to be published in a Nature journal.

Major Strengths:
None noted.

Minor strengths:
1. The paper showed a new updated list of cusp crossings, updating the field of this well-studied phenomenon at Saturn’s magnetosphere.
2. The paper compares MHD simulations of Saturn to the Cassini dataset, and then to a simulation of the Earth.

Major weaknesses:
1. The paper does not provide a substantial original contribution to the field (see remarks above about originality and significance).
2. The paper did not make a compelling case that it is identifying more accurate cusp crossings instead of reproducing previous work. The authors claim that in their Figure R9 “Our identification is more accurate, excluding the periods when the spacecraft had clearly entered lobe region between the second and the third red dashed line”, citing that the cusp example shown in their figure is a more accurate identification of previously identified cusps. However, the same identification of the two cusp events is identified in the same manner as previous publications. Jasinski et al., (2016) who the authors cite, separate their cusp and show the two cusp identifications in their online supporting material (just as the authors have done here). Arridge et al., (2016) identify the two cusp crossings also, for the same interval, in their Figure 9, in exactly the same manner as Jasinski et al., (2016) as well as how the authors are identifying it. The same is true for the authors Figure R9. Therefore, the authors are not producing more accurate identification but instead reproducing previous work.

Minor weaknesses:
1. The authors claim that “The magnetopause reconnection at Saturn is more sensitive to east-west component of IMF but not north-south component” however then later contradict that this is can be true when they write a few sentences later that “due to the limited availability of simultaneous solar wind monitoring data from in-situ observations of Saturn’s and Jupiter’s magnetospheres” . Furthermore, lobe reconnection cusp identification can be completed by analyzing the ion dispersions in the dataset.
2. Figure 1 in the paper shows a magnetospheric sketch of Saturn with the cusp labelled with a question mark (i.e. “Cusp?”), implying that this phenomenon is being identified for the first time. Considering previous publications that have reported cusp observations (e.g. Jasinski et al., 2014, 2016, 2017; Arridge et al., 2016) this labeling is misleading.

Zhang et al. (2021) reported an important work who first revealed Jupiter’s complex three-
dimensional magnetic topology through high-resolution simulations. Their study showed that
much of Jupiter’s polar cap is threaded by helical magnetic flux that closes within the planetary
interior, extends into the outer magnetosphere, and accumulates near the dawn flank, where
strong differential plasma rotation drags field lines sunward, as shown in Figure R1. In addition,
they found that open magnetic field regions extend unusually far into the dusk and nightside
sectors, fundamentally challenging the traditional noon-centered cusp paradigm derived from
terrestrial observations. This work has had a significant impact within the planetary science
community, and NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory has since identified further exploration of
Jupiter’s three-dimensional magnetospheric structure as a primary objective of Juno’s second
extended mission (Bolton et al., 2025).
Figure R1. Jupiter’s complex three-dimensional magnetic field structure was first revealed by
Zhang et al. (2021) using high-precision, low-dissipation simulations. Unlike traditional
magnetic field models, this framework successfully explains the persistently bright polar
auroras observed at Jupiter, which differ fundamentally from Earth’s auroral morphology.
Building on this foundation, Chen et al. (2023) demonstrated that magnetopause
reconnection at Jupiter is primarily controlled by the east–west component of the interplanetary
magnetic field, rather than the north–south component dominant at Earth, with reconnection
occurring predominantly at high latitudes, as shown in Figure R2. Xu et al. (2024) subsequently

 Distinction from Previous Saturn Asymmetry Studies:
As the referee mentioned, we fully acknowledge that previous Cassini observations have
revealed pervasive asymmetries throughout Saturn's magnetosphere (e.g., Pilkington et al.,
2015; Jia & Kivelson, 2016; Wilson et al., 2013; Sergis et al., 2017; Allen et al., 2018), which
can be divided into two main categories:
(1) Within the Magnetodisc Region: Numerous studies documented asymmetric plasma
flow patterns (Wilson et al., 2017; Thomsen et al., 2014; Kane et al., 2014), with dawn-side
outward and dusk-side inward radial velocities. Particle distributions show pronounced
asymmetries, with energetic particle pressure exhibiting a midnight maximum to noon
minimum ratio of ~5 (Arridge et al., 2015; Sergis et al., 2017). Allen et al. (2018) revealed that
water group ions prefer the dusk-to-premidnight sector, while H⁺ and H₂⁺ show dual-flank
enhancement. Geometrical asymmetries include plasma sheet thinning from noon to midnight
(Krimigis et al., 2007) and stronger ring currents in the dusk-to-midnight sector (Kellett et al.,
2011);
(2) At High-Latitude Boundaries: Pilkington et al. (2015) found the dawn-side
magnetopause extends 7±1% farther than other regions. Jia & Kivelson (2016) simulations
showed dawn-side expansion arising from differential plasma expansion/contraction rates
along rotating flux tubes.
As comprehensively reviewed by Arridge et al. (2015), these asymmetries have been
interpreted within two main theoretical frameworks:
1. Solar wind–driven models: The framework of Cowley et al. (2003, 2005), which
combines the Vasyliūnas and Dungey cycles, predicts dusk-side Vasyliūnas X-lines
and dawn-side Dungey X-lines, shown by Figure R4. Although this framework is
consistent with some observations, direct evidence for such X-lines remains limited.
An alternative is the viscous interaction model (Delamere & Bagenal, 2010, 2013),
which does not require large-scale convection.
2. Rotational dynamics models: The model proposed by Kivelson and Southwood (2005)
attributes the asymmetry to firehose instability in the dusk-side plasma sheet, an
interpretation supported by simulations demonstrating the development of pressure
anisotropy (Vogt et al., 2014).
Despite these frameworks, fundamental questions remained unanswered:
 The detailed magnetic field topology of giant planet magnetospheres remains
incompletely understood, and previous simulation studies have not adequately
illustrated how magnetic connectivity between the magnetosphere and the solar wind
is established (Jia & Kivelson, 2016).
 The suppression of low-latitude magnetopause reconnection at Saturn (Lai et al., 2012;
Fuselier et al., 2014, 2020; Jasinski et al., 2021) contradicted expectations from Dungey
cycle models (Cowley et al.; 2003, 2005).
How Our Work Advences This Understanding:
Our study takes a further step toward understanding the giant planet picture linked to these
critical gaps by revealing, for the first time:
1. The Detailed Magnetic Topology Picture: Our high-resolution GAMERA
simulations (Zhang et al., 2019) demonstrate Saturn's global magnetic field
configuration, showing how open field lines extend to the post-dusk sector—a
configuration not very likely to to predict from previous frameworks based on Earth-
like reconnection. The post-dusk cusp extension we observe is closely associated with
this high-latitude reconnection geometry. The dawn-side magnetopause expansion
noted by Pilkington et al. (2015) and Jia & Kivelson (2016) now can be potentially
understood as part of the global magnetic topology we revealt.
2. The Magnetopause Reconnection Geometry: We show that Saturn's magnetopause
reconnection occurs predominantly at high latitudes, governed by the east-west IMF
component rather than north-south as in Dungey models. This explains why low-
latitude reconnection is suppressed—it's not an anomaly but a fundamental
characteristic of the system.
3. Cross-Planetary Comparison: By demonstrating that Saturn exhibits the same
reconnection pattern recently discovered at Jupiter (Chen et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024),
as well as exhibiting location distributions and particle characteristics closely
resembling those of Jupiter’s post-dusk cusp events we establish this as a fundamental
characteristic of rapidly rotating magnetospheres, not a planet-specific anomaly. This
strong correspondence indicates similar cusp microphysics across giant planets and
highlights a distinct pattern of magnetosphere–solar wind interactions in giant planets,
fundamentally different from those at Earth.
In essence, although previous studies have thoroughly documented asymmetries in
Saturn’s magnetosphere, our work advances understanding by proposing a framework
that can account for the suppression of low-latitude reconnection at Saturn—a feature
not adequately explained by Dungey cycle–dominated models. Through combined
observational and simulation-based evidence of Saturn’s magnetic topology (e.g., cusp
regions), we provide a helpful framework for interpreting these asymmetries.

 Ion Dispersion at Earth
At Earth, ion dispersion in the cusp has been extensively studied and provides clear
diagnostics of magnetopause reconnection modes (e.g., Cargill et al., 2005; Pitout et al.,
2006; Lockwood & Smith, 1994). These dispersion patterns arise from the combined
effects of (1) convection of newly reconnected field lines and (2) the energy-dependent
travel times of ions along magnetic field lines, often referred to as velocity filtering
(Lockwood & Smith, 1994).
Consider a situation that a spacecraft traversing the cusp from lower to higher latitudes.
Under southward interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) conditions, when subsolar
reconnection dominates through the classical Dungey cycle, a spacecraft traversing the
cusp from lower to higher latitudes encounters progressively older/later open field lines.
This produces normal ion dispersion, in which high-energy ions are observed first on
younger/new-generated field lines near the equatorward boundary, followed by
progressively lower-energy ions on older field lines toward the polar cap. In contrast,
under northward IMF conditions, high-latitude lobe reconnection can occur, leading to
reversed or anomalous dispersion as the spacecraft encounters the newest reconnected
field lines at higher latitudes.
This direct relationship between dispersion signatures and reconnection modes is effective
at Earth because (1) the magnetosphere is strongly controlled by the solar wind, (2) the
reconnection picture is relatively simple, typically involving subsolar versus lobe
reconnection, and (3) the associated field-line convection patterns are well constrained
(Lockwood & Smith, 1994; Pitout & Bogdanova, 2021; Smith & Lockwood, 1996).
 More Complex Picture at Giant Planets

the similarity between the magnetopause reconnection configuration of Saturn’s

Given that our study reveals Saturn's magnetopause reconnection geometry closely resembles
Jupiter's—with high-latitude reconnection controlled by east-west IMF components rather than
north-south—we expect similar complexity in ion dispersion patterns at Saturn.
Overall, the following factors make ion dispersion analysis challenging for Saturn dataset:
(1) At rapidly rotating giant planets, rapid planetary rotation generates complex convection
patterns that vary strongly with local time and radial distance. Convection speeds can
change substantially across the cusp region, and the observed ion dispersion depends
sensitively on the spacecraft trajectory relative to these moving structures. Unlike Earth,
where solar wind conditions largely control convection, giant planets are dominated by
intrinsic rotational dynamics that govern field line motion. Moreover, Saturn's 10.6-hour
rotation period drives strong azimuthal flows that vary with radial distance and local time,
creating spatially variable convection velocities that change the relative motion between
spacecraft and field lines;
(2) Lack of upstream solar wind monitoring: Without simultaneous solar wind measurements,
we cannot determine the IMF orientation during each cusp crossing, making it impossible
to predict expected dispersion patterns.
In conclusion, while ion dispersion analysis is a helpful tool, the combination of rapid rotation,
complex reconnection geometry, and lack of solar wind monitoring makes this approach
difficult for determining reconnection modes at Saturn. Although detailed ion dispersion
analysis is beyond the scope of this work, it represents an important future research direction

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Saturn’s magnetosphere, shaped by solar wind interaction with its dipole field, differs from Earth’s due to faster rotation and Enceladus’s internal plasma sources. An ongoing focus of investigation is how the internal plasma sources and rapid rotation result in a different global magnetospheric configuration. The magnetospheric cusp, a crucial interaction region between solar wind and planetary magnetic field, serves as an indicator of global magnetic configuration. Here we utilize Cassini observations from 2004 to 2010 to study dawn-dusk asymmetry in Saturn’s cusp distribution and extend the number of cusp events from about 11 reported in previous studies to 67. We find peak occurrence in the post-noon sector and signatures extending to post-dusk (near 20 local time), resembling recent observations of Jupiter’s post-dusk cusp. We further examine magnetic topology using high-resolution magnetohydrodynamics simulations to visualize the cusp asymmetry. This is consistent with previous studies, but our simulations provide a more detailed view of Saturn’s magnetic topology near the magnetopause. This asymmetry of cusp distribution demonstrates how rapid rotation and internal plasma sources fundamentally alter magnetospheric configuration, offering insights for understanding other rotating planetary systems within and beyond the solar system.

---

## Introduction

Planetary magnetospheres are formed as a result of the continuous interaction between the high-speed solar wind and the internally generated magnetic fields present in most planets within the solar system, which display considerable variations among different planets. For example, the magnetospheres of Jupiter and Saturn are more internally driven because of the planets’ rapid rotation speeds coupled with internal plasma sources within their magnetospheres, which differs from the strongly solar wind-driven magnetospheres typically seen on Earth1,2. In the case of ice giants like Uranus and Neptune, the unique pole-on configuration of their magnetospheres – the geometry in which the upstream solar-wind flow is approximately aligned with the planet’s magnetic dipole axis – lead to distinct coupling dynamics with the solar wind3,4. Atthesametime,the highly dynamic nature of these gas giants’ plasma environments fosters complex interactions with the solar wind, which serves as an external factor in the magnetospheric dynamics5,6. Understanding these diverse magnetospheric dynamics can improve the interpretation of observations of planetary systems and offer useful perspectives for the broader field of planetary science, including star-planet interactions.

When the solar wind interacts with a planetary magnetosphere, magnetic reconnection on the magnetopause often occurs where the magnetic shear is sufficiently large. At Earth, magnetopause reconnection is strongly governed by the north–south component of the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF)—with southward IMF driving subsolar reconnection and northward IMF favoring high-latitude lobe reconnection7. In the rotationally dominated magnetospheres of giant planets, magnetopause reconnection was reported to be favored at high latitudes. In contrast, low-latitude subsolar reconnection is often suppressed by diamagnetic effects and is therefore less likely to occur there8–10. Recent simulations11–13 have suggested that reconnection at Jupiter is strongly influenced by the east–west IMF component, with reconnection occurring predominantly at high latitudes and suppressed reconnection at low-latitude magnetopause locations. During reconnection, solar wind particles are allowed to enter the magnetosphere through the newly reconnected magnetic field lines. The magnetospheric cusp is known as a vital funnel-shaped region that permit these particles to directly access the atmosphere14,15. The cusps play a crucial role in planetary magnetospheres, as they significantly contribute to various mass and energy transport processes within the magnetosphere, ionosphere, and upper atmosphere. These processes are key in the formation of geomagnetic storms16, substorms17, and auroras18. A series of in situ studies, e.g., using the Cluster multi-spacecraft mission, have revealed that Earth’s cusp is a broad, complex region characterized by various intriguing boundary layers14,19. The cusp in Earth’s quiescent magnetosphere, strongly governed by solar wind, typically exhibits a general morning-afternoon symmetry of its morphology and statistical occurrence rates, which is one of the most fundamental properties of terrestrial cusp20,21, although the distribution of its spatial location can be influenced by the IMF By component and pressure of the solar wind22,23. In contrast, due to Saturn’s rapid rotation, the Kronian magnetospheric plasma generally subcorotates relative to the planet, remaining in near-rigid corotation within approximately 20 Rs, but falling significantly below the rigid corotation rate beyond Titan’s orbit24,25. Compared to Earth, Jupiter exhibits bright and persistent polar auroras26, and Saturn’s aurora shows variable morphologies resembling both Earth-like and Jupiter-like structures27, suggesting a markedly different magnetospheric configuration and dynamics of rapidly rotating giant planets2,28,29. The rapid rotation of giant planets plays a crucial role in modifying magnetic flux transport within the magnetosphere and near the magnetopause compared to Earth12,29. This rotational influence can modify dawnside magnetopause reconnection rates associated with solar wind interaction and alter the configuration of the magnetopause and the open–closed field line boundary, where the cusps are anchored12,29.

Zhang et al.11,29 provide additional insights into the distinct magnetospheric configurations of Earth and giant planets using high-resolution simulations. In rotation-dominated Jovian-like systems, low reconnection rates on the dawn side can cause closed flux to accumulate there, resulting in an open flux fraction of approximately 20% in the polar region (above 80° magnetic latitude, MLAT20). Conversely, a terrestrial-like magnetosphere is mostly solar wind-dominated, exhibiting near-complete openness of the polar region above 80° MLAT (about 98%)29. Although Saturn’s magnetosphere is similarly rotation-dominated, its weak magnetic field (an equatorial magnetic field strength of 0.21 G, about 1/20 of Jupiter’s30) results in its reduced corotation dominance. The consequently higher solar wind merging potential-to-corotation potential ratio (0.38 at Saturn vs. 0.09 at Jupiter29) increases solar wind-driven flux opening efficiency. As a result, Kronian-like magnetosphere’s polar open flux fraction varies widely (58–93% above 80° MLAT)29. Observationally, Saturn’s high-latitude magnetosphere has been reported to be largely plasma-depleted and composed predominantly of open field lines, with the polar cap boundary located at 14.5 ± 0.6° and 12.7 ± 0.6° colatitude in the southern and northern hemispheres, respectively31,32. Compared to Jupiter’s small open flux area, Saturn’s relatively large area of open magnetic field may result in a more observable cusp, although more detailed analysis and observations are needed to confirm the prediction. Previous theoretical models by Cowley et al. (2004, 2005)33,34 proposed that rotational dynamics drive the subsolar X-line at Saturn, thereby influencing the azimuthal distribution of the polar cap and cusp in local time. This framework is based on terrestrial magnetopause reconnection pictures and the Dungey7/Vasyliūnas cycle35. However, the applicability of the Dungey cycle to giant planets remains a topic of active debate36.

Currently, the global distribution picture of Saturn’s cusp remains an active topic of ongoing research. As shown in the simple schematic Fig. 1, a comparative analysis of Saturn’s cusp distribution with Earth’s is crucial for understanding the diverse planetary magnetospheres and their interaction with the solar wind.

Some case studies have identified characteristics in Saturn’s cusp region, such as magnetosheath-like electron features and ion dispersion patterns that are similar to those observed in Earth’s cusp37–40. Additionally, variations in ion dispersion features under different reconnection conditions and magnetic depression features in Saturn’s cusp have been examined, revealing parallels with Earth’s cusp37,38,40. These similarities indicate that the microphysical processes governing the behavior of charged particles within cusps might be universal across different planetary environments. However, the study by Arridge et al.40 noted cusp encounters recurring in sync with Saturn’s rotation period, thought to be linked to the cusp position oscillating in phase with Saturn’s global magnetospheric dynamics40. Previous research utilizing global magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations has demonstrated that the magnetospheric structure of rapidly rotating giant planets exhibits significant asymmetries41, markedly different from those observed at Earth11,12. For instance, simulation studies have shown that rapid rotation significantly alters the global magnetospheric configuration of Jupiter, notably causing a pronounced duskward shift in the open magnetic field regions associated with Jupiter’s polar cusp11,12. This dusk-side distribution of Jupiter’s cusp has been supported by observational results from Xu et al. (2024)13. Given Saturn’s rotation-dominated magnetosphere, a similar duskward shift in its cusp distribution is expected13,29.

However, several questions remain unresolved. A comprehensive global observational picture of cusp regions at giant planets is still lacking. At Jupiter, due to Juno’s current orbital constraints13,42,43, high-latitude observations in the middle-to-outer magnetosphere across various local times remain incomplete, leaving the properties and distribution of cusp regions in the dawn, noon, and post-noon sectors mysterious. Given Saturn’s similarly rapidly rotating magnetosphere, investigating its global cusp distribution is especially important. Such research provides valuable comparative insight into Jupiter’s reported dusk-side cusp and informs future observations of Jupiter’s cusp and high-latitude boundary layer regions. Previous studies have provided valuable analyses of several Saturn cusp events37–40. Here we extend this foundation by offering a global, dwell-time–normalized statistical view, enabling a global assessment of the cusp occurrence distribution.

In the present research, we explored the global distribution of Saturn’s cusp using data from the Cassini spacecraft, spanning from 2004 to 2010. Additionally, we employed high-resolution MHD simulations11,12,44 to visualize the magnetic configurations of Saturn and its cusp, revealing Saturn’s magnetopause-related three-dimensional magnetic topology. Both the statistical analysis and the simulation results highlight the characteristics of the morning-afternoon asymmetry in Saturn’s cusp, which diverges from the symmetric distribution observed at Earth and shows consistency with Jupiter’s recently discovered configuration.

---

## Results

A Kronian cusp case is presented for the period between 23:00 on January 30 and 05:00 on January 31, 2009, when the Cassini spacecraft was located in the high latitude (>40°) noon region of the northern hemisphere, near 16 Rs (Fig. 2). Cassini transitioned from the magnetospheric region to the boundary layer and the cusp region, as shown in Fig. 2. In this study, we examine Cassini’s in-situ measurements from three key sources: the Cassini Magnetometer instrument (MAG)45, Cassini Plasma Spectrometer - Electron Spectrometer (CAPS-ELS)46, and Cassini Plasma Spectrometer - Ion Mass Spectrometer (CAPS-IMS)46. Before 23:51 UT, as indicated by the first dashed line in Fig. 2, Cassini recorded a magnetospheric electron spectrum with enhanced energy ranges between 1000 and 10000 eV. In this region, the ion energy spectrum displayed no distinct features, and the electron pitch angle distribution was isotropic. These characteristics are indicative of the magnetosphere at this location30,40; hence, this region is identified as part of the magnetosphere and is denoted by the letter M in Fig. 2.

After 00:36 UT marked by the second dashed line in Fig. 2, the spacecraft observed a region characterized by a notable enhancement in the electron energy spectrum from 10 to 100 eV, as depicted in Fig. 2c. This enhancement is characteristic of magnetosheath electrons47. Concurrently, the magnetic field component remained relatively stable, as shown in Fig. 2a, b, which rules out the possibility of the spacecraft being in the magnetosheath. Additionally, observations included a bidirectional distribution of low-energy electrons and a rise in high-energy electrons opposing the magnetic field direction (shown in Fig. 2e–h), along with multiple ion dispersion signals. These observations suggest that the magnetopause experienced pulsed reconnection processes37,48. These distinct features robustly indicate that the region encountered by the spacecraft is indeed a magnetospheric cusp region37,38,40. Situated between the magnetosphere and the cusp is a transitional area, characterized by plasma properties that are intermediate between those of the magnetosphere and the cusp. This region is identified as a boundary layer and is denoted by BL in Fig. 2.

To identify Kronian cusp events, the most important criteria, based on previous research on Saturn’s cusp37,38,40 and Jupiter’s cusp13, are as follows: (1) Spacecraft location, e.g., relatively high latitudes (>30 degrees) and within the magnetopause; (2) Most typical plasma characteristics within cusp regions, e.g., magnetosheath-like electron energy distributions13,37,38,40. These are the Level 1 criteria, the most critical for identification. Most Saturn cusp events can be well identified by meeting these criteria. Additionally, other important but non-essential features can further aid in identification, including ion dispersion37,40 associated with magnetopause reconnection, field-aligned electron distributions37,40, and magnetic depressions39 within cusp regions. These are referred to as the Level 2 criteria, which can be helpful but are not necessary for cusp identification. Utilizing all these criteria, we identified a total of 67 cusp events that matched the characteristics observed by the Cassini spacecraft between 2004 and 2010. These events encompass previously reported cases of Saturn’s cusp region, demonstrating the reliability of our identification and the consistency of this study with prior research. Information on Saturn’s cusp events and the corresponding criteria fulfillment is organized in the Supplementary Data 1. It is noted that the survey period of 2004–2010 corresponds to the timeframe from Cassini’s entry into Saturn’s bow shock to the final year before the CAPS instrument was placed in Operations on Hold (2011)38. Since the detection of magnetosheath-like electron spectra by CAPS provides the most direct and essential evidence for cusp identification14,20,40, data collected after 2011 were excluded to ensure the reliability of event identification. This study does not distinguish between cusp types associated with different magnetopause reconnection pictures. Recent findings suggest that magnetopause reconnection at giant planets may be significantly more complex than the subsolar/lobe-dominated patterns observed at Earth, with reconnection-related dynamics exhibiting greater variability11–13. Moreover, long-term, stable solar wind measurements are lacking at Saturn during the Cassini mission39,40, and solar wind models cannot provide real-time, accurate information on the east–west and north–south components of IMF39,40,49. As a result, identifying cusp types based on ion dispersion signatures linked to specific reconnection geometries is highly challenging and beyond the scope of this study.

The global distribution of these events is presented in Fig. 3. Fig. 3a and b demonstrate that the majority of observed cusp events are located in the northern hemisphere and predominantly on the afternoon side, with some events even detectable on the post-dusk side (after 20 local time, LT). Fig. 3c displays the distribution of cusp events at high latitudes (>30° or <-30°) across various radial distances and local times. Due to the Cassini spacecraft’s trajectory constraints, its high-latitude path in the southern hemisphere is primarily on the morning side, while in the northern hemisphere, it is largely on the afternoon side. Notably, between radial distances of 10 and 20 Rs, high-latitude tracks are present on both the morning and afternoon sides. However, there is a marked contrast in event density for 10 to 20 Rs radial range in high latitudes (Fig. 3c). Between 13 and 16 LT, a total of 17 cusp events were identified within Cassini’s accumulated dwell time of 36,626 minutes, corresponding to an event density of approximately 0.028 events per hour. In contrast, during the interval from 8 to 11 LT with a dwell time of 37,379 minutes, only 4 cusp events were detected, indicating a substantially lower event density of 0.006 events/hour. Although previous studies have reported minor differences in the period of kilometric radiation waves north and south of Saturn50,51, there is currently insufficient evidence to suggest a pronounced north-south asymmetry in Saturn’s magnetospheric configuration that can notably impact the polar cusp structure. Thus, this study posits that the observed distribution reflects the morning and afternoon asymmetry in Saturn’s cusp distribution. More importantly, three post-dusk cusp events were identified during the statistical study, with the specific identification criteria for each event detailed in Supplementary Data 1. And comprehensive plasma analyses, along with comparisons distinguishing these events from nightside ionospheric outflows, are provided in Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Figs. 1–3. The plasma energy spectra and spatial distributions of these events closely resemble those observed in Jupiter’s post-dusk polar cusp region as reported by Xu et al. (2024) (see Supplementary Note 1), indicating a consistent cusp microphysics and complex magnetospheric structures across different giant planets.

To quantify this asymmetry, we computed the probability distribution of the cusp with the time resolution of 1 minute, as depicted in Fig. 4b. Additionally, for comparative purposes with Saturn, we replicated Earth’s cusp probability distribution using the Cluster electron and magnetic field datasets52 as shown in Fig. 4a. It is noted that the cusp detections at different local times are normalized by the spacecraft’s high-latitude dwell time at corresponding local times for both Cluster and Cassini, minimizing potential statistical biases caused by orbital differences. For detailed information on event identification and case presentations in Earth’s cusp region, please refer to Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Fig. 4. The results of this distribution are consistent with previous studies20: The peak occurrence rate of Earth’s cusp is centered around noon (11-13 LT), with some disparity between the morning and afternoon sides, which can be attributed to the influence of the IMF By component and solar wind dynamic pressure, which can shift and modify the cusp’s position during spacecraft observation22,23. In contrast, the peak occurrence rate of Saturn’s cusp manifests on the afternoon side 13-15 LT. Notably, Saturn’s cusp distribution does not mirror the shift of Earth’s cusp distribution toward the afternoon under positive IMF By condition22. Instead, it shows a clear shift in overall distribution toward the dusk or even the night side. Global MHD simulations11,29,44, as illustrated in Fig. 4c and 4d, map the magnetic field configurations near the magnetopauses of Earth and Saturn, highlighting the differences between their distributions. Saturn’s magnetopause, influenced by the planet’s rapid rotational dynamics, is more expanded on the morning side compared to the afternoon side, in agreement with previous MHD simulations and observations, which found the magnetopause was typically expanded by 1-2 Rs on the dawn side compared to dusk41,53,54. The cusp must conform to this topology, leading to the observed asymmetry and enabling cusp observation even on the post-dusk side — an occurrence hardly seen at Earth20,22. Moreover, the simulation results reveal a picture of Saturn’s magnetopause reconnection under typical solar wind conditions, which closely resembles that of Jupiter12,13. Reconnection occurs predominantly at high latitudes and is suppressed in low-latitude magnetopause regions—unlike Earth, where reconnection is primarily governed by the north–south component of the interplanetary magnetic field7,14,55. For a detailed presentation and analysis of Saturn’s magnetopause reconnection results, please refer to Supplementary Note 3 and Supplementary Figs. 5–6.

---

## Methods

Simulation information
In this study, the global MHD model of Saturn’s magnetic configuration (Fig. 4d) is built upon the GAMERA code (Grid Agnostic MHD for Extended Research Applications) to tackle equations on a specifically designed curvilinear, non-orthogonal grid suited for the study of planetary magnetospheres44. The computational model employs a 256 × 256 × 256-cell grid, implemented as a non uniform, distorted spherical grid oriented along the Solar Magnetic (SM) X-axis and possessing a symmetry axis. The grid exhibits non-uniformity in the radial-azimuthal plane, with cell sizes reducing as they approach Saturn. The simulation begins at an inner boundary of 4 Rs, with boundary conditions obtained from electrostatic potential models61,62. The outer boundary takes the form of a cylinder, stretching from SM-X = 56 Rs to SM-X = -600 Rs, with a radius around 214 Rs. The conditions at this outer boundary are controlled by the solar wind and the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF). The grid is structured so that its resolution diminishes with increasing distance from Saturn, which enhances computational efficiency by aligning with the larger scale of magnetospheric processes farther from the planet. The radial cell sizes near Saturn’s magnetopause range between approximately 0.1 and 0.2 Rs. This model is driven by simplified representations of solar wind and IMF conditions, setting IMF Bz at -0.5 nT, a particle density of 0.1 per cubic centimeter, a solar wind velocity of 400 km/s. The dipole tilt of Saturn’s magnetic field is maintained at 0 degrees to remove hemispheric asymmetries, thereby simplifying the overall analysis. Moreover, the moon Enceladus ejects plasma into Saturn’s magnetosphere63,64, creating an internal plasma source that migrates outward and influences the magnetopause. The simulation data presented in this paper are publicly available online via Xu (2026)65.

Cassini and cluster data
We analyzed magnetometer (MAG), electron spectrometer (ELS), and ion mass spectrometer (IMS) data from the Cassini spacecraft spanning 2004-2010. Data were obtained from the NASA Planetary Data System. We analyzed magnetic field observations and position data from the Cassini MAG instrument45, and thermal ion and electron measurements with energy ranges up to 28 keV (electrons) and 50 keV (ions) from Cassini-CAPS/IMS/ELS46. Cluster magnetic field and particle data were obtained from the ESA Cluster Science Archive. The datasets to analyze Earth’s cusp were obtained by the FGM66, PEACE67, CIS68, and WHISPER69 instruments onboard Cluster. Detailed identification information of Earth’s cusp is shown in Supplementary Note 2.

Data availability
All Cassini data presented here are publicly available from NASA’s Planetary Data System (https://pds-ppi.igpp.ucla.edu/). The MAG dataset of Cassini is available via https://search-pdsppi.igpp.ucla.edu/search/view/?f=yes&id=pds://PPI/cassini-mag-cal. The CAPS dataset of Cassini is available via https://search-pdsppi.igpp.ucla.edu/search/?sc=Cassini&i=CAPS. The Cluster data used in this paper can be obtained from the Cluster Science Archive via https://csa.esac.esa.int/csa-web/. The simulation data of Saturn’s magnetospheric topology presented in this paper are publicly available online via Xu (2026)65 https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/RQJYH. The datasets generated during and/or analysed during the current study are available from the corresponding author upon request.

Code availability
The Cassini data are processed and analyzed using the Spedas package70, which can be downloaded via the https://github.com/spedaspage. The presentation of simulated data can be done using standard plotting libraries (Python/Matlab), for example, the Python library matplotlib (which can be downloaded via the https://matplotlib.org/stable/install/page). The Matlab code used in the analysis of simulations is publicly available online via Xu (2026)65 https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/RQJYH.
